idiom_name: interface ElementVisitor<R> with overloaded visit() methods and an abstract adapter
implementation_notes: The textbook Java form: an abstract Visitor with one visitX overload per concrete element, an Element interface with accept(Visitor), and a one-line override in every concrete element that calls the matching overload - overload resolution happens on the static type of this, which is the second dispatch. Because adding an element forces every visitor to change, ship an abstract adapter that implements all methods (no-op or delegation) and extend that. The JDK uses exactly this shape in javax.lang.model.element (ElementVisitor plus AbstractElementVisitor / ElementKindVisitor / ElementScanner) and documents the central weakness in the same breath: new language constructs add methods to the interface, so classes that implement ElementVisitor directly are source-incompatible with future releases. On Java 21 a closed hierarchy can instead be sealed and each operation written as an exhaustive switch.
pitfalls: Implementing accept() once in a base class with instanceof checks: the static type at the callback is the base class, so the overload cannot be resolved and the double dispatch is lost.

Adding an element type breaks every visitor at once; implement through abstract adapters (AbstractElementVisitor-style) instead of the interface, and expect the source-incompatible edit when a new element kind arrives.
Visitors that remove elements during the walk throw ConcurrentModificationException from the collection iterator or skip subtrees; collect edits and apply them after the traversal.
Allocating one visitor per traversal is normal, but sharing a stateful visitor between threads is not: keep the state in the visitor instance and never reuse it across concurrent walks.

variants.name: Sealed interface + exhaustive switch expression (pattern matching)
variants.idiom_name: sealed interface with records + exhaustive switch (JEP 409 / JEP 441)
variants.implementation_notes: With Java 21 the compiler can enumerate the permitted subtypes of a sealed interface and prove that a switch covers them, so each operation becomes one method with a switch expression and the accept()/visit() machinery disappears; the nodes lose their dependency on an operation interface entirely. The maintenance cost does not vanish, it moves: adding a subtype makes every switch over the hierarchy non-exhaustive and the build fails with a precise list - the same work a visitor forces, with less boilerplate and no adapter classes. Keep the classic visitor when the hierarchy is third-party or not sealable, when operations must be classes that plugins implement, or when several teams compile against the operation interface.
pitfalls: Sealing cannot be retrofitted onto a hierarchy you do not own, and a non-sealed subtype reopens the set; the technique only applies to types you control.

A switch that was exhaustive at compile time throws MatchException at run time if the sealed hierarchy is recompiled without recompiling the switch - recompile the whole module after changing the hierarchy.
Every operation now repeats the switch over the hierarchy; for a deep recursive structure the traversal still needs a shared walker, so the pattern can reappear at the walk level.
Records expose their state through accessors, but pattern matching tempts call sites into ad-hoc logic - keep each operation a named method so the switch stays in one place.
